newsitem.title: USA: Koreas trade barbs but talks said to make progress.
newsitem.headline: Koreas trade barbs but talks said to make progress.

text.p: North and South Korea traded accusations on Thursday before holding a third session of talks with China and the United States to prepare for negotiations on a permanent peace for the Korean peninsula.

The communist Pyongyang government blasted the United States and South Korea for planning joint military exercises later this month, and Seoul said demands by North Korea were preventing progress in this week's talks. In Washington, State Department spokesman James Rubin dismissed the criticism of the joint exercises.
"We do not regard actions we take with regard to South Korea as threatening," he said. "On the contrary, we have a defence alliance, not an offence alliance, with South Korea."

He added: "We are comfortable that we have done all we can in preparing for these talks to create a climate in which success can occur. If people want to find excuses for not making progress, they can. But the climate is fine."

The talks, which began on Tuesday, are aimed at setting a date, place and agenda for formal negotiations to replace the 1950-53 Korean War armistice with a more durable peace agreement, possibly in the form of a treaty.

As officials met on Thursday, North Korea's Vice-Minister of Foreign Affairs Kim Gye Guan told reporters: "We are making some progress. No promises yet ... There have been some differences of opinion."

The talks had proceeded "quite smartly", Rubin said. "They have made some progress on items such as a date and a venue for the next meeting, but no final decisions have been made. I think they're getting back to capitals on that."
Asked about reports the substantive talks would be held in Geneva, Rubin, speaking at a State Department briefing in Washington, only advised reporters not to make hotel reservations in New York.

China was North Korea's ally in the Korean War and the United States supported the South. An armistice signed by the parties to end the fighting did not technically end the war and Korea remains the last flashpoint of the Cold War.

"They (the U.S. and South Korea) are talking peace but if they are going to act against the process with these war drills, then there is no reason for communication and the talks have no meaning," Radio Pyongyang quoted a North Korean spokesman from the Committee for the Peaceful Reunification of the Fatherland as saying on Thursday.

The U.S.-South Korean exercise is scheduled for Aug. 18 to 29 and involves 16,500 U.S. military personnel and tens of thousands of South Koreans. The joint drills have been conducted every year since 1976.
The Seoul government said on Thursday that Pyongyang's demands for the withdrawal of American troops and for a peace deal with Washington alone had impeded progress in the talks.

"It is absurd that they have agreed to hold four-nation talks to discuss peace and then say a peace arrangement be made only with the U.S.," South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman Lee Kyu-hyung said.

About 37,000 U.S. troops are stationed in South Korea to help defend the country, and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday that Washington would not consider Pyongyang's request. "We are not going to do that," she said.
South Korea remained hopeful the four countries would open substantive negotiations sometime this year aimed at forging a permanent peace for the bitterly divided peninsula.
"I would not rule out a breakthrough but it is quite unlikely," Lee said when asked whether the New York delegations could manage to set an agenda within this week.
This week's meetings marked an important phase in the complex relationship between the four countries because it was the first time representatives of China had joined the talks.
The Chinese delegation said Beijing was "positive" about establishing a peace arrangement and supported reconciliation between North and South.
